title: Contained κατὰ λέξιν or in substance — Trinity proves the point
source_text: VIII. Igitur quae sint illa, quae Scriptura sacra contineri dicimus, ex dictis manifestum est. Deinceps videndum est, qua ratione & modo ex sententia nostra in Scriptura contineantur. Porro dogmata & praecepta quaedam in aliquo libro possunt contineri duobus modis. Primo quidem κατὰ λέξιν, & iisdem verbis. Secundo in substantia, & verbis aequipollentibus. Nostra autem sententia non est omnia fidei dogmata, atque vitae praecepta quae traduntur ab orthodoxis, totidem verbis in sacra Scriptura reperiri. Istud quidem nobis imputant hodierni quidam vitilitigatores, qui ex eo quod profitemur nihil nos extra Scripturam in religionis negotio suscipere, exigunt ut quaecunque scribimus & docemus, totidem verbis & syllabis in Scriptura sacra ostendamus. Verum nobis sufficit ad credendum aliquod dogma, ut Scriptura sacra illud in substantia contineat. Ita Scriptura Sacra nullibi habet haec verba, Deus est unus & trinus. Et tamen illud certa fide credimus, quin quod eodem recidit Scriptura dicit tres esse in caelo, Patrem, Verbum, & Spiritum, & hos tres unum esse. Et pluribus in locis testatur Deum esse unum, & tamen Patrem esse Deum, Filium esse Deum, & Spiritum sanctum esse Deum.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore what those things are which we say are contained by sacred Scripture is plain from what has been said. Next it is to be seen by what reason and mode, according to our opinion, they are contained in Scripture. Further, certain dogmas and precepts can be contained in some book in two ways. First indeed κατὰ λέξιν, and in the same words. Second in substance, and in equivalent words. But our opinion is not that all dogmas of faith, and precepts of life which are handed down by the orthodox, are found in so many words in sacred Scripture. That indeed certain modern wranglers impute to us, who from the fact that we profess that we take up nothing outside Scripture in the business of religion, demand that whatever we write and teach we show in so many words and syllables in sacred Scripture. But it is enough for us, for believing some dogma, that sacred Scripture contain it in substance. Thus sacred Scripture nowhere has these words, God is one and three. And yet we believe that with certain faith, inasmuch as Scripture says what comes to the same, that there are three in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and these three are one. And in many places it testifies that God is one, and yet that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God.
pass_b_english: From the above it is clear what we say Scripture contains. Next: how it contains them.
Dogmas and precepts may stand in a book in two ways — first κατὰ λέξιν, in the same words; second in substance, in equivalent words.

We do not claim every orthodox dogma and life-precept appears in Scripture in so many words. Some modern wranglers pin that on us: because we take up nothing outside Scripture in religion, they demand every sentence we teach be shown syllable by syllable in the text.

For us it is enough that Scripture contain the dogma in substance. Scripture nowhere says the bare words ‘God is one and three’; yet we believe it firmly, because Scripture says what comes to the same — three in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and these three are one — and in many places that God is one, while the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each God.
